title: Why an extreme poverty line is still needed
gist: World Bank economists defend the $3-per-day extreme poverty line against proposals to abandon or raise it, arguing that with 826 million still in extreme poverty, collapsing aid budgets, and the bottom 10% seeing near-zero income growth, a very low line remains essential to direct scarce attention and resources to the world's poorest.

insights.claim: The World Bank's international extreme poverty line is currently set at $3 per person per day in 2021 prices and underpins the first target of the Sustainable Development Goals.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The $3 line is the official global poverty benchmark, so debates over changing it directly reshape how development progress is measured and funded.
insights.quote: currently set at $3 per person per day in 2021 prices

insights.claim: The share of the global population in extreme poverty has fallen from 43% in 1990 to 10% today, with China, India, Indonesia, and Brazil now at 4% or lower and over one hundred economies below 1%.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The historic decline is what fuels calls to retire the line, framing the authors' defense as pushing against a strengthening consensus.
insights.quote: The share of the global population in extreme poverty has fallen from 43% in 1990 to 10% today.

insights.claim: Two recent scholarly proposals suggest supplementing the extreme poverty line with a threshold 10 to 15 times higher.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Concrete competing proposals define the policy fight the authors are contesting over how global poverty is benchmarked.
insights.quote: Two recent proposals suggest supplementing the line with a threshold 10 times or 15 times higher.

insights.claim: In relatable terms the $3 line equals about $675 per month or $8,100 per year in 2026 prices for a typical six-person poor household measured by consumption, corresponding to roughly $10,000 a year in income.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Translating the abstract daily figure into household budgets counters the criticism that the line is unrealistically low.
insights.quote: the international poverty line comes to $675 per month ($8,100 per year).

insights.claim: An estimated 826 million people still live in extreme poverty, a population larger than the European Union and United States combined, with dozens of countries still above 40%.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The absolute count shows the goal is far from achieved, rebutting the 'last mile' argument for raising ambition.
insights.quote: an estimated 826 million people still live in extreme poverty—a population larger than the European Union and the United States combined.

insights.claim: If the highest-poverty countries develop at the typical historical pace it would take at least three generations to reach 3%, and the poorest are currently progressing far slower than historically, so the number of extreme poor could rise over the coming decade.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A potential reversal in extreme-poverty numbers signals that development trajectories in the poorest states are deteriorating, not converging.
insights.quote: If this continues, the number of extreme poor could rise over the coming decade.

insights.claim: Raising the global poverty line to $30 per day would at the margin shift attention to countries like Slovakia and Hungary, and at $45 to Czechia and Poland.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A higher line mechanically redirects poverty focus toward middle-income Europe, diluting attention on the truly destitute.
insights.quote: Raising the poverty line to $30 per day would at the margin shift attention to countries such as Slovakia and Hungary

insights.claim: The bottom 10% of the global population grew their incomes just 0.1% annually over the last decade while those in the middle grew 2% annually, so the very poorest are falling further behind.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Near-zero growth at the bottom versus 2% in the middle is the core evidence that the poorest need a dedicated benchmark all their own.
insights.quote: The bottom 10% of the global population have seen virtually no progress over the last decade, growing their incomes 0.1% annually, while those in the middle of the global distribution have grown by 2% annually

insights.claim: Low-income countries receive one-hundredth the media coverage of high-income countries and one-tenth that of upper-middle-income countries.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Structural attention scarcity for poor countries justifies a metric that deliberately keeps focus on them.
insights.quote: low-income countries receive 1/100th of the attention of high-income countries and 1/10th that of upper-middle income countries in media coverage.

insights.claim: With global Official Development Assistance down roughly 30% over the last two years, even channeling all ODA to effective targeted cash transfers would cover only a third of the budget needed to end extreme poverty.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A 30% aid collapse against a threefold funding shortfall makes prioritizing the very poorest a fiscal necessity, not a preference.
insights.quote: even if all ODA was channeled to highly effective cash transfers targeted to those in extreme poverty, we would only have a third of the budget necessary to end extreme poverty

insights.claim: The World Bank's extreme poverty line has since inception been anchored to the national poverty lines of the poorest countries, which are calibrated around the cost of meeting basic food and shelter needs.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Significantly raising or lowering the line detaches it from how the poorest societies themselves define poverty, an argument for methodological restraint.
insights.quote: the World Bank’s extreme poverty line has been determined by the national poverty lines of the poorest countries.
